Abstract This special issue, Advancement in Computational Fluid Mechanics: Bridging Theory and Appli-
cation, presents a curated set of studies that exemplify the continuing evolution of Computational Fluid
Mechanics (CFM) as both a scientiﬁc discipline and an engineering tool. The contributions cover an exten-
sive range of ﬂow phenomena and modeling scales, encompassing magnetohydrodynamic and nanoﬂuid
convection, multiphase and interfacial dynamics, turbulent reacting ﬂows, hemodynamic transport in bio-
logical systems, and ﬂow–structure interactions in complex geometries. Together, these works demon-
strate how advanced numerical frameworks such as lattice Boltzmann and immersed boundary formula-
tions, hybrid RANS–LES turbulence models, AI-assisted and optimization-driven simulations, and data-
integrated reduced-order modeling are enabling unprecedented predictive capability across domains from
propulsion and energy systems to biomedical and microﬂuidic devices. Several studies highlight the growing
integration of machine learning and high-performance computing to accelerate model calibration, enhance
physical ﬁdelity, and uncover new parametric insights. Collectively, the articles reinforce the central vision
of this collection: to bridge rigorous theoretical development with application-driven problem solving,
thereby transforming CFM from a traditional analysis tool into a unifying framework for innovation in
science, technology, and design.
1 Introduction
Computational Fluid Mechanics (CFM) has evolved from a specialist’s numerical tool into a cornerstone of modern
engineering and applied science. The growth of high-performance computing and multi-physics algorithms now
enables the simulation of ﬂows that couple turbulence, heat and mass transfer, electromagnetic forces, phase change,
and reactive chemistry across a vast range of scales. CFM has become indispensable to innovation in propulsion,
energy systems, and biomedical and microﬂuidic applications, where accurate and interpretable predictions are
crucial for design and optimization. Yet, the enduring challenge remains to bridge rigorous theoretical development
with the practical demands of robustness, eﬃciency, and physical ﬁdelity. This special issue on “Advancement
in Computational Fluid Mechanics: Bridging Theory and Application” addresses this intersection, presenting 42
contributions that illustrate the ﬁeld’s breadth from magnetohydrodynamic and nanoﬂuid convection to reacting,
multiphase, and bio-hemodynamic ﬂows while emphasizing the growing synergy between computation, physics,
and data.
The articles collectively capture the transformation of CFM into a predictive, design-enabling framework. Studies
on magneto-nanoﬂuid systems [1–5] elucidate electromagnetic control of heat transfer, while energy and propul-
sion works advance modeling of jet plumes, injector dynamics, and turbomachinery performance. Investigations
into droplet breakup, coalescence, and multiphase transport [6–8] demonstrate interface-resolved precision, and
biomedical applications [9, 10] reveal CFD’s power to probe nanoparticle-laden blood ﬂow and arterial mechanics.
Complementary eﬀorts on algorithmic innovation, spanning Haar wavelet solvers, lattice Boltzmann formulations,
hybrid AI–SPH simulations, and evolutionary optimization [11–13] highlight the fusion of physics-based modeling
with data-driven computation.

Collectively, these contributions capture the essence of this Topical Collection: the convergence of theory, com-
putation, and application in contemporary ﬂuid mechanics. They reveal a discipline that continues to expand
horizontally by integrating new physics such as magneto-, electro-, and bio-hydrodynamics and vertically, by
reﬁning the numerical backbone that supports predictive simulation. More importantly, they demonstrate that
CFM has matured beyond being a diagnostic tool; it now functions as a unifying platform for discovery, design,
and innovation. Through these diverse studies, this collection underscores the transformative role of computa-
tion in unraveling complex ﬂow behavior, informing real-world engineering, and guiding the next generation of
multidisciplinary modeling in science and technology.
2 Applications in various systems
2.1 Magnetohydrodynamic and nanoﬂuid systems
One theme of this issue concerns heat and mass transfer in magnetically inﬂuenced and nanoﬂuidic systems, where
electromagnetic eﬀects and nanoparticle suspensions are exploited to enhance energy transport and control ﬂow
behavior. Studies on ferroﬂuid convection and entropy generation in trapezoidal or elliptical domains [4, 5, 14]
explore the interplay between magnetic ﬁeld orientation, buoyancy forces, and thermal gradients. Investigations on
hybrid Cu–water and ferro-nanoﬂuid ﬂows [1, 5] highlight magnetic ﬁeld tuning as an eﬃcient means of improving
heat transfer in energy storage and battery-cooling applications. These contributions underscore how CFM enables
the exploration of complex coupled transport mechanisms that are otherwise diﬃcult to capture experimentally.
2.2 Energy systems, combustion, and propulsion
Several contributions focus on combustion, propulsion, and energy conversion systems, demonstrating the role of
CFD in optimizing performance and reducing emissions. Enhanced Electric Vehicle Battery Cooling Using Hybrid
Nanoﬂuids [15], infrared emission studies of non-axisymmetric jet plumes [16] and ﬂamelet-based simulations of
piloted methane/air turbulent ﬂames [17, 18] reveal the ﬁne-scale coupling between ﬂow structure and radiative
behavior. Numerical analyses of LOx–methane swirl injectors [19], spray–wall interaction in gasoline direct injec-
tion [20], soot coagulation in diesel engine exhaust [21], and the eﬀect of liquid-to-gas density ratio on atomizer
performance [22] highlight the continued reﬁnement of multiphase combustion modeling. Investigations of turbo-
fan performance scaling [23], static-Stall prediction of airfoils at high Reynolds numbers [24], serpentine nozzle
aerodynamics [25], inﬂuence of blade, hub, and nacelle modeling on propeller–wing interactions [26], and the
combined eﬀect of swirl strength and injector position on micro-gas turbine combustor behavior [27] emphasize
computation’s growing role in aerospace system design. Complementary studies on VAWT cluster optimization [28]
and jet impingement cooling of curved surfaces [29] extend CFM’s application to renewable energy and thermal
management domains.
2.3 Multiphase, interface, and shock-driven ﬂows
High-ﬁdelity modeling of multiphase and interfacial phenomena remains a core strength of CFM. Contributions
addressing capillary pinch-oﬀin immiscible systems [6], oscillating bubble coalescence [8], mixing performance
dependence on diametric ratios and inclination angles in cross-Stream ﬂows [30], mixed and natural convection
in power-law ﬂuids inside a square enclosure [31], HAM solution of chemically reactive radiative Casson ﬂuid
ﬂow [32], circular pattern by continuous deposition of liquid threads onto a moving substrate [33], two-phase
ﬂow by varying the sparger shape and orientation [34], and surfactant-laden transport via lattice Boltzmann
methods [35] demonstrate the ability of CFM to capture dynamic interfacial behavior with high precision. Studies
on droplet deformation under thermal gradients [7], shock–particle interactions [36], and hydro-abrasive erosion
modeling in turbine systems [37] showcase advanced numerical methods for transient and high-gradient ﬂows.
These investigations collectively highlight how interface-resolving and high-resolution schemes enable deeper insight
into ﬂow topology, breakup mechanisms, and material erosion processes relevant to industrial and environmental
systems.
2.4 Biomedical and bioﬂuid dynamics
Biomedical applications of CFD are rapidly expanding, driven by its capability to simulate complex physiological
ﬂows that are challenging to measure in vivo. Several studies in this issue model hemodynamics and nanoparticle-
laden blood ﬂow through stenosed or curved arteries [9, 10], revealing how wall elasticity, pulsatility, and nanopar-
ticle concentration inﬂuence shear stress and arterial health. Other works examine the eﬀect of heart rate variations

on arterial pressure and stress ﬁelds [9], blood ﬂow and mass transport in stenosed arteries [38], and the coupling
of convective and diﬀusive transport in realistic coronary geometries [10]. At smaller scales, hybrid electroosmotic
and magnetically actuated microﬂows [39] demonstrate CFD’s role in designing eﬃcient microﬂuidic mixers and
diagnostic devices. Together, these contributions reinforce the growing integration of computational methods into
biomedical research and healthcare technology development.
2.5 Mathematical modeling, AI, and optimization frameworks
The ﬁnal group of papers focuses on algorithmic and mathematical innovation, showcasing how emerging numeri-
cal techniques and AI-assisted approaches are transforming CFD workﬂows. The collocation-based Haar wavelet
method for transonic and weak-shock problems [11], the hybrid ISPH–AI simulation of nanoﬂuid convection [12],
and path graph polynomial matrix formulations for boundary value problems [40] exemplify this methodological
evolution. Optimization and data-driven frameworks, including NSGA-II-based airfoil performance design [13],
synthetic surface reconstruction for additive manufacturing [41], and ﬂow optimization in corrugated microchan-
nels [42], illustrate the synergy between machine learning and computational physics. Collectively, these studies
highlight that the frontier of CFM now lies in hybridizing physical modeling with algorithmic intelligence to achieve
both eﬃciency and ﬁdelity.
3 Why this collection and what comes next
This Topical Collection serves as a resource for academics, industry scientists, engineers, and researchers interested
in leveraging CFM to address challenges spanning propulsion, energy, bioﬂuidics, and emerging multi-physics
systems. The 42 papers in this collection reﬂect a discipline in dynamic evolution, one that has matured in
numerical rigor while expanding in physical breadth and application depth. From nanoscale thermal transport
to high-speed propulsion and physiological ﬂows, these works collectively demonstrate how CFM uniﬁes theory,
computation, and experimentation into a single predictive framework. Across these diverse topics, several cross-
cutting lessons emerge:
a.
Modeling ﬁdelity often matters most where you least expect it: in hubs, nacelles, surface curvature,
or roughness maps.
b.
Coupling is the norm: chemistry with turbulence, electromagnetics with convection, interfacial transport
with hydrodynamics, and the heartbeat with wall stress.
c.
CFD for design is most eﬀective when methods and models are chosen because the physics
demand it, not because the method is fashionable.
Collectively, the papers in this Topical Collection exemplify this ethos.
We are grateful to the authors for tackling substantive problems with methodological rigor, to the reviewers for
their careful and constructive assessments, and to the editorial oﬃce for its guidance. The guest editors hope that
this collection serves as a reference and inspiration for future research that continues to bridge fundamental ﬂuid
dynamics with real-world technological innovation, reinforcing the role of CFM as both a scientiﬁc instrument and
a design engine for the modern era.
